Dense Reconstruction of Degraded Scenes from Sparse Views
A. Author, B. Author, C. Author

Abstract
We present a dense reconstruction method for scenes observed under degraded imaging conditions. The central observation is that the weighting between photometric and geometric residuals should depend on the estimated reliability of each pixel rather than on a global constant. We derive the weighting from a per-pixel variance proxy and integrate it into the standard differentiable rendering loop, adding no trainable parameters. Experiments on three datasets show consistent improvement in the low-visibility regime while leaving the clean regime essentially unchanged. Code and configurations are released with the paper.I. Introduction
We study reconstruction under degraded imaging conditions and report what changes when the observation model is degraded. The setting assumes 8 calibrated views with overlapping coverage, and the reconstruction is optimised jointly over geometry and appearance so that both terms are updated from the same residual. Our treatment keeps the optimiser identical to the baseline and changes only the residual weighting, which lets the effect of the weighting be isolated from any other implementation detail. Every claim below is evaluated under the same protocol, and negative results are reported alongside positive ones because the failure cases are the part that transfers to other scenes. We deliberately keep the evaluation narrow: a single protocol applied to every model, with the same number of iterations and the same resolution, so that a difference in the table reflects the method and not the tuning budget. Where a baseline is known to be sensitive to one of these choices we report both settings and mark which one we treat as primary.

IV. Implementation
We implement the residual weighting as a small module inserted between the rasteriser and the loss. We train all models on a single RTX 4090 for 30k iterations, and we use the same schedule for every baseline so that the comparison is not confounded by tuning effort. The per-pixel variance proxy is computed once per iteration from the rasteriser output, which costs less than two percent of the total iteration time.V. Experiments
A. Setup
We set the learning rate = 1e-4 and the batch size = 4 for all models, and we fix iterations = 30000. The resolution is kept at 800 pixels on the long side. Baselines are re-run under the identical protocol; where a baseline publishes a different configuration we report both numbers and note the difference rather than silently using the stronger one.

Where a baseline is known to be sensitive to one of these choices we report both settings and mark which one we treat as primary.VI. Limitations
We do not evaluate on real underwater sequences, so the claim that the weighting transfers to physical degradation remains untested. The variance proxy also assumes independence between neighbouring pixels, which is false near object boundaries.

VII. Conclusion
We study what the results do and do not establish and report what changes when the observation model is degraded. The setting assumes 11 calibrated views with overlapping coverage, and the reconstruction is optimised jointly over geometry and appearance so that both terms are updated from the same residual. Our treatment keeps the optimiser identical to the baseline and changes only the residual weighting, which lets the effect of the weighting be isolated from any other implementation detail. Every claim below is evaluated under the same protocol, and negative results are reported alongside positive ones because the failure cases are the part that transfers to other scenes. We deliberately keep the evaluation narrow: a single protocol applied to every model, with the same number of iterations and the same resolution, so that a difference in the table reflects the method and not the tuning budget.
